title: Prediction models of medical checkup according to types of disability: a cross-sectional study

detail.title: Prediction models of medical checkup according to types of disability: a cross-sectional study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Conflict of Interests: The author declared that no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical Approval: This study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institution Review Board (IRB) of Dongyang University (exemption No. 1041495-202403-HR-06-01). This study used secondary data from the 4th Disability and Life Dynamics Panel (DLDP), which is collected and publicly distributed by the Korea Institute for Health and Social Affairs (KIHASA)/ Korea Disabled People’s Development Institute(KODDI).

detail.abstract: This study aimed to develop a prediction model for medical checkup participation among people with disabilities using decision tree analysis. Utilizing cross-sectional secondary data from Korea’s Disability and Life Dynamics Panel, the analysis identified key factors associated with lower participation rates across disability types. Among individuals with physical disabilities, those without children and experiencing a lower-than-average impact of disability showed the lowest checkup rates. Women with brain lesions who rarely met acquaintances and had low disability acceptance demonstrated the lowest participation within their group. For people with visual disabilities, reduced family strength and long travel time to hospitals were associated with minimal checkup engagement. Among individuals with hearing disabilities, those not economically active and reporting low family strength had the lowest rates. Overall, satisfaction with medical services, social interaction frequency, disability acceptance, disability severity, depression, family support, and economic activity emerged as influential predictors of medical checkup participation.

title: Sticky Prices and Constraints to Produce
affiliations: University College London, University College London and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Sticky Prices and Constraints to Produce
detail.abstract: We study whether firms in medium-scale New Keynesian models  would voluntarily satisfy demand at their posted prices, or whether  nominal rigidities may push prices below marginal costs. In the  Altig et al (2011) framework, which features full indexation of  non-adjusting prices and wages to steady-state inflation and near  constant returns to scale at the firm level, we find that violations  of firms' willingness-to-supply condition are negligible: fewer than  one percent of firms are ever constrained, and the associated output  losses are tiny. Two features of the model drive this result: marginal  costs that are nearly unresponsive to output, and prices that adjust  more frequently than wages. When the short-run marginal-cost  schedule is sufficiently steep, willingness-to-supply violations become quantitatively relevant. Our findings thus characterize the  conditions under which the standard demand-determination assumption is a reliable approximation and those under which it may not be.

title: The Green Comparative Advantage. Divergent Trade Trajectories to the EU CBAM Reporting Phase in Latin America
affiliations: Tsinghua University and Duke Kunshan University

detail.title: The Green Comparative Advantage. Divergent Trade Trajectories to the EU CBAM Reporting Phase in Latin America
detail.abstract: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is a policy designed to equalize carbon costs between European producers and imported goods. It began with a reporting phase (October 2023-December 2025) in which importers disclosed embedded emissions but paid nothing. We ask whether this phase changed Latin American exports to the EU. We propose that, before carbon is priced, trade should respond only where exporters combine low embedded emissions with the capacity to document them. We test this with a triple-difference PPML gravity model on HS6 bilateral trade from ten Latin American exporters from 2017 to 2024 (3.1 million observations). The design compares CBAM-covered with non-covered products, EU with non-EU destinations, and 2024 with 2017-2022. We find no aggregate EU-specific change in covered exports. The response is confined to aluminum, whose EU-bound exports rose by about 280% relative to non-covered goods. Shipment volumes drive the increase, while unit values do not change. The estimate is stable across single-exporter exclusions, fixed-effect choices, and an earlier pre-period. Steel, cement, and fertilizer show no EU-specific response. This work provides early empirical evidence on trade-pattern adjustments during CBAM’s implementation.

detail.abstract: Multimodal speech-based systems that combine acoustic and linguistic information have achieved promising performance in Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection. Strong classification performance on clean data does not, however, establish that the acoustic evidence exploited by such systems remains stable when the speech waveform is perturbed. This study systematically evaluates the adversarial robustness of three representative multimodal AD detection models. We perturb only the speech waveform of AD samples and examine whether the models can be induced to classify these samples as healthy controls (HCs) across different multimodal fusion mechanisms. To this end, we introduce a pathological-acoustic-basis-guided (PABG) attack, which derives four waveform-level perturbation bases from AD-associated acoustic characteristics, uses them for score-guided initialization, and subsequently refines the perturbation through constrained momentum-based optimization. In the white-box setting, all three models prove highly sensitive to targeted adversarial perturbations. Even for the most robust model, the false-negative rate (FNR) rises from 12.6\% to 78.6\% at a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 23.0~dB. Cross-model transfer experiments further show that the generated adversarial examples remain effective across different fusion architectures. Query-based black-box evaluations reveal pronounced architecture-dependent robustness, with the word-level aligned model showing markedly greater resistance within the prescribed perturbation budget. These findings underline the need for explicit robustness assessment and effective defenses before multimodal speech-based AD detection systems are deployed in real-world settings.

title: More than being customer: Brand Capital and Trade Credit
affiliations: Jilin University (JLU), Yunnan University of Finance and Economics, Peking University HSBC Business School and ShanghaiTech University

detail.title: More than being customer: Brand Capital and Trade Credit

affiliations.org_name: Yunnan University of Finance and Economics
affiliations.preferred_name: Yunnan University of Finance and Economics

detail.abstract: We examine the relationship between brand capital and trade credit financing. Using Chinese listed firms from 2011 to 2023, we find that brand capital is positively associated with trade credit financing. The effect is stronger among firms in regions with higher marketization, greater environmental uncertainty, lower asset specificity, and longer organizational decline, while customer volatility weakens the relationship. Further analyses show that suppliers value both the accumulated value of brand capital and the future cash flows associated with it. The positive association is also stronger when product market similarity is higher, suggesting that competition-related advertising may reinforce brand recognition rather than simply represent wasteful spending. Our results are robust to alternative measures and endogeneity tests. We further find that greater trade credit financing is associated with higher subsequent total factor productivity.

detail.abstract: This short note considers the neglected question of whether consumers (as opposed to consumers plus arbitrage agent) benefit from arbitrage activities in the form of storage and interconnection, In the case of electricity storage, the answer is that in current circumstances it is very likely to be beneficial to them. The case of interconnection is somewhat more moot.

title: Collapsing economies and endogenous takeoff in unified growth theory
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Auckland Business School, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Collapsing economies and endogenous takeoff in unified growth theory

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: We provide a global characterization of the dynamics of the Galor--Weil--Lagerlöf model for unified growth theory. We show that the model possesses the following features: the canonical transition from Malthusian stagnation to modern growth is not a global outcome but rather a local property that depends on the initial states of the economy; large sets of initial states lead to population collapse; the Malthusian trap is not a steady state of the system and thus cannot attract economies in the long run; Lagerlöof's calibration lies at a border-collision bifurcation that generates a continuum of steady states in the sustained growth regime. Motivated by these properties, we construct a smooth model that admits both a Malthusian steady state and a locally stable sustained growth regime. In contrast to the Galor--Weil--Lagerlöf specification, different initial states of the proposed smooth model can lead to population collapse, permanent stagnation, or endogenous takeoff.
